RETAIL SALES
FORECASTING


Model evaluation, feature drivers, and business decision insights





                                             FINAL PRODUCTION MODEL


          Gradient Boosting Regressor





Portfolio analysis report | Prepared from supplied project artifacts

Retail Sales Forecasting


01 Executive Summary


 Gradient Boosting was selected as the final production model after evaluation on a held-out future test

 period. It achieved the lowest reported final-test MAE and RMSE and the highest R2 when compared with

 the tuned XGBoost alternative.


   67.27      214.09     65.66%     0.9704


          FINAL MAE                   FINAL RMSE                  FINAL SMAPE                   FINAL R2



  Decision             The model explains approximately 97% of outcome variance on the
  takeaway             reported held-out test period, but the high SMAPE indicates that
                          percentage error remains material for low-volume series.



 What the model is learning

 Lagged sales and rolling averages dominate the importance ranking. The top three inputs -

 rolling_mean_7, lag_7, and lag_1 - account for 77.9% of total reported importance. This confirms that

 recent demand history is the primary predictive signal.

 Recommended use

 Deploy forecasts as decision support for replenishment, procurement, promotion planning, and

 store-level review. Monitor error by store and product family, and retain human review for unusual

 events or low-volume items.

 Feature design reflected in the model

 The feature set combines recent lags (1, 7, 14, and 28 days), rolling means and variability, expanding

 history, calendar fields, promotions, holidays, store identifiers, and product-family indicators. This is

 appropriate for a retail panel where both temporal dynamics and cross-sectional differences matter.

 Evaluation design

 The supplied narrative describes a held-out future test period. This is preferable to a random split for

 forecasting because it more closely represents how predictions will be used after deployment and

 reduces temporal leakage risk.

03 Candidate Model Benchmark


 Six candidate models were compared on the supplied validation results. No single model dominated

 every metric: Random Forest produced the lowest validation MAE and SMAPE, while Gradient Boosting

 produced the lowest validation RMSE and highest R2.





  Model                     MAE            RMSE             SMAPE            R2

   Linear Regression                93.84             340.55            99.35%             0.9375

   Decision Tree                   102.12            462.07            59.36%             0.8850

  Random Forest                  69.87             298.13            57.04%             0.9521

   Gradient Boosting                72.72             290.10            61.85%             0.9547

   HistGradientBoosting             72.94             296.89            61.33%             0.9525

  XGBoost                        71.20             312.48            60.74%             0.9474

04 Final Held-out Test Decision


 The final artifacts compare Gradient Boosting with a tuned XGBoost model on the held-out test period.

 Gradient Boosting wins on all four reported metrics and is therefore the justified production choice.





  Model                       MAE            RMSE             SMAPE            R2

   Gradient Boosting                   67.27             214.09            65.66%             0.9704

  Tuned XGBoost                     72.24             235.40            68.81%             0.9642



 Measured advantage

 Relative to tuned XGBoost, Gradient Boosting reduces MAE by 4.97 units (6.9%) and RMSE by 21.31 units

 (9.1%). Its R2 is higher by 0.0062.

 Interpretation caution

 The business_analysis artifact reports a tuned XGBoost validation RMSE of 295.65, while the

 final_test_results file reports an RMSE of 235.40. These values appear to represent different evaluation

 stages. They are preserved separately in this report and are not treated as interchangeable.

05 Forecast Drivers





   77.9%      91.1%      40.6%      22.4%


       TOP 3 SHARE               TOP 5 SHARE              ROLLING MEAN 7                LAG 7



 The concentration in lag and rolling features indicates strong persistence and weekly recurrence.

 Calendar, holiday, promotion, store, and family indicators add incremental signal, but their individual

 importance is much smaller in this fitted model.

 Operational implication

 Reliable and timely historical sales feeds are more important than any single auxiliary field. Data-quality

 monitoring should prioritize missing dates, late sales records, duplicate transactions, and leakage in

 rolling calculations.

 Deployment recommendation

 Deploy the Gradient Boosting model as a monitored decision-support service. Produce forecasts on a

 fixed schedule, retain prediction timestamps and model versions, and compare realized sales with

 forecasts as data arrives.



   Monitoring layer               Recommended measure

   Overall accuracy                MAE, RMSE, SMAPE, and R2 by forecast horizon

  Segment accuracy                  Error by store, product family, and promotion status

   Bias                        Mean signed error to detect persistent over- or under-forecasting

  Data quality                       Missing dates, stale inputs, unusual lags, and schema changes

  Model drift                           Rolling comparison against naive and seasonal baselines

07 Limitations and Next Steps


 1. External economic variables and unexpected events are not represented in the supplied feature

 summary.

 2. Accuracy varies across stores and product families; aggregate metrics can conceal weak segments.

 3. The reported SMAPE remains high despite strong R2, so low-volume series require special attention.

 4. Promotion features show predictive association but do not establish causal lift.

 5. Dataset dimensions, date range, missing-value counts, bias, and store/category rankings were blank in

 the supplied narrative files.



 Prioritized next steps


   Priority      Action                                           Expected value

  1         Add store-family error and bias dashboards.          Expose where aggregate performance is misleading.

             Benchmark against naive and seasonal-naive
  2                                                             Prove incremental business value.

  4         Add external variables where available.

  5          Automate retraining and drift alerts.                   Maintain accuracy as demand patterns change.



 Final recommendation

 Proceed with Gradient Boosting as the production baseline. Treat the system as a forecast assistant, not

 an autonomous inventory controller, until segment-level monitoring, bias analysis, and baseline

 comparisons are complete.

 Metric definitions


   Metric                    Interpretation

  MAE                  Average absolute forecast error in target units; lower is better.

  RMSE                   Square-root mean squared error; penalizes large misses more heavily.

  SMAPE                Symmetric percentage error; can remain volatile around small actual values.

  R2                    Share of target variance explained relative to a mean baseline; higher is better.



 Reporting note

  All numerical claims originate from the supplied files or are arithmetic comparisons derived directly from

 them. Blank source fields were not inferred. Validation and final-test results are presented as separate

 evaluation stages.
